    P1: Pred = lambda w: 0 in w[0]
    P2: Pred = lambda w: 1 in w[0]
    left = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P1)(v)) or P2(v))(w0)
    right = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P2)(v)) or P1(v))(w0)
    print("      .3  □(□p→q) ∨ □(□q→p) at S=∅: %s ∨ %s = %s   ->  FAILS"
          % (left, right, left or right))

    # the mixed tense axiom p → □ ◇̌ p is valid on the same frame
    tense_ok = all(
        (not P(w)) or box(ws, gdia(ws, P))(w)
        for P in all_predicates(ws)
        for w in ws
    )
    print("   mixed tense axiom p → □◇̌p (ground modality): %s" % tense_ok)
    print("      => bimodal separation: □◇̌ valid while □◇ (Brouwer) fails")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 5 -- derived buttons and derived CH branches
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_buttons_and_branches(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. DERIVED BUTTONS AND DERIVED CH BRANCHES")
    print("=" * 74)
    positive = [
        atom("btn", 0),
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        conj(TRU, disj(atom("btn", 0), conj(atom("btn", 1), atom("btn", 0)))),
    ]
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    for f in positive:
        # Boolean-valued monotonicity along the stage order
        for S, T in product(_stages(n), _stages(n)):
            if S <= T:
                vs = bval(f, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
                vt = bval(f, make_assignment(T, n, m), m)
                assert vs & ~vt == 0, (show(f), S, T)
        # the resulting button law in the frame
        assert all(
            (not csat(w, f)) or csat(v, f)
            for w, v in product(ws, ws)
            if accessible(w, v)
        )
        print("   %-42s is a button (monotone Boolean value)" % show(f))

    ch = atom("sw", 0)  # the designated CH switch
    for S in _stages(n):
        value = bval(ch, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
        assert value != 0 and value != top_mask(m)
    print("   ⟦CH⟧_S is neither ⊥ nor ⊤ at every stage -> branching theorem applies")
    for w in ws:
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: csat(v, ch))(w)
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: not csat(v, ch))(w)
    print("   ◇CH ∧ ◇¬CH holds at every one of the %d worlds: CH is a switch" % len(ws))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 6 -- the invariant fragment theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def button_free_normal_form(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Substitute ⊥ for every button atom: the canonical button-free candidate."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return p
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return FLS if p[1][0] == "btn" else p
    return imp(button_free_normal_form(p[1]), button_free_normal_form(p[2]))


def is_invariant(p: Formula, n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Does the truth value of p depend only on the switch setting?"""
    for g in generic_objects(m):
        values = {csat((S, g), p) for S in _stages(n)}
        if len(values) > 1:
            return False
    return True


def demo_invariant_fragment(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. INVARIANT FRAGMENT THEOREM:  invariance ⟺ button-free normal form")
    print("=" * 74)
    tests = [
        atom("sw", 0),
        imp(atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)),
        atom("btn", 0),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), neg(atom("btn", 0))),          # a tautology: invariant
        imp(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 0)),                # invariant
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0)),                # not invariant
    ]
    for p in tests:
        inv = is_invariant(p, n, m)
        nf = button_free_normal_form(p)
        agrees = all(
            csat((S, g), p) == csat((S, g), nf)
            for S in _stages(n)
            for g in generic_objects(m)
        )
        assert inv == agrees, show(p)
        print("   %-28s invariant=%-5s  normal form %-22s agrees=%s"
              % (show(p), inv, show(nf), agrees))
    print("   (equality of the two columns is exactly the fragment theorem)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 7 -- exact criterion for two-sided branch preservation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def survives_both_branches(background: int, value: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥ -- necessary and sufficient."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    return (background & value) != 0 and (background & full & ~value) != 0


def demo_branch_preservation(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. BRANCH PRESERVATION:  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥")
    print("=" * 74)
    stage = frozenset({0})
    assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
    ch = atom("sw", 0)
    value = bval(ch, assign, m)
    cases = {
        "button background  ⟦b0⟧ (b0 pushed)": bval(atom("btn", 0), assign, m),
        "trivial background ⊤": top_mask(m),
        "switch background  ⟦s0⟧ = ⟦CH⟧": value,
        "opposite switch    ⟦¬s0⟧": bval(neg(ch), assign, m),
        "unpushed button    ⟦b1⟧": bval(atom("btn", 1), assign, m),
    }
    for name, b in cases.items():
        print("   %-38s  b=%-8s survives both CH branches: %s"
              % (name, bin(b), survives_both_branches(b, value, m)))
    print("   -> button-definable backgrounds branch; switch-entangled ones cannot,")
    print("      and an inconsistent background (⊥) branches vacuously nowhere.")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 8 -- counting the frame:  3^n · 4^m accessibility pairs
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def count_accessibility_pairs(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of the pairs (w,v) with w ⊑ v."""
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    return sum(1 for w, v in product(ws, ws) if accessible(w, v))


def demo_counting(max_n: int = 3, max_m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. EXACT SIZE OF THE FORCING RELATION:  |⊑| = 3^n · 4^m")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    n  m   worlds 2^(n+m)   brute force   3^n·4^m   match")
    for n in range(max_n + 1):
        for m in range(max_m + 1):
            if n + m > 5:
                continue
            brute = count_accessibility_pairs(n, m)
            closed = 3 ** n * 4 ** m
            assert brute == closed
            print("   %2d %2d   %12d   %11d   %7d   %s"
                  % (n, m, 2 ** (n + m), brute, closed, brute == closed))
    print("   three states per button (off/off, off/on, on/on -- never on/off),")
    print("   four per switch (its value before and after are unconstrained).")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  helpers
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def _stages(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """All 2^n stages (sets of pushed buttons)."""
    return [
        frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)
    ]


def _sample_formulas(n: int, m: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """A spread of test formulas mixing button and switch atoms."""
    b0, b1 = atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", min(1, n - 1))
    s0, s1 = atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", min(1, m - 1))
    return [
        FLS,
        TRU,
        b0,
        s0,
        neg(b0),
        neg(s0),
        imp(b0, s0),
        conj(b0, s0),
        disj(b0, s0),
        conj(disj(b0, b1), neg(s1)),
        imp(conj(s0, s1), disj(b0, neg(b1))),
    ]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("BOOLEAN-VALUED REALIZATION OF THE FORCING MULTIVERSE -- NUMERICAL DEMOS")
    print()
    demo_forcing_closure()
    demo_truth_lemma()
    demo_realization()
    demo_frame_logic()
    demo_buttons_and_branches()
    demo_invariant_fragment()
    demo_branch_preservation()
    demo_counting()
    print("all checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Exhaustive Finite Verification of the Boolean-Valued Realization
demos.description: A self-contained suite of eight demonstrations that checks, by exhaustive finite computation on control frames with a handful of buttons and switches, every theorem of the development: (1) forcing closure, i.e. that the Hilbert axioms and further classical tautologies all receive Boolean value top at every stage while a switch atom receives an intermediate value; (2) the truth lemma for principal generic filters, verified over all stages, all generic objects and a spread of test formulas; (3) the realization theorem, comparing two-valued truth at each control world with membership of the generic object in the stage-wise Boolean value; (4) the frame laws together with brute-force validity of T, 4 and .2 over all 2^|W| predicates and explicit refutation of the axioms 5, B and .3; (5) monotonicity of Boolean values for the positive button fragment, hence the derived button law, plus the derived Continuum-Hypothesis branching; (6) the invariant fragment theorem, comparing exhaustive invariance testing against the button-free normal form; (7) the exact two-sided branch-preservation criterion applied to button-definable and switch-entangled backgrounds; and (8) the closed form 3^n * 4^m for the number of accessibility pairs, checked against brute-force enumeration.
demos.code:
"""
Numerical demonstrations for:

    An Internal Boolean-Valued Realization of the Forcing Multiverse

Everything is self-contained: no third-party dependencies, no imports beyond the
standard library.  Running the file executes eight demonstrations, each of which
checks -- by exhaustive finite computation -- one of the theorems of the paper.

Objects modelled
----------------
*   Control worlds  (S, g)   with  S ⊆ {0..n-1}  a set of *pushed buttons*
    (irreversible) and  g ∈ {0,1}^m  a setting of the *switches* (free).
    Accessibility:  (S,g) ⊑ (T,h)  iff  S ⊆ T.

*   Boolean algebra  B = P(G)  where  G = {0,1}^m  is the space of generic
    objects.  Elements of B are represented as integer bitmasks of width 2^m.

*   Boolean values ⟦p⟧_S of propositional assertions at stage S, generic
    filters, generic quotients, forcing.

Checks performed
----------------
1.  Forcing closure: every classical tautology has Boolean value ⊤.
2.  Truth lemma:  quot(v,U) ⊨ p   iff   ⟦p⟧ ∈ U.
3.  Realization theorem:  (S,g) ⊨ p  iff  g ∈ ⟦p⟧_S.
4.  Frame laws + S4.2 soundness; failure of 5, of Brouwer, and of linearity .3.
5.  Derived buttons (positive button fragment) and derived CH branches.
6.  Invariant fragment theorem: invariance  ⟺  button-free normal form.
7.  Branch-preservation criterion  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧^c ≠ ⊥.
8.  Exact count of accessibility pairs:  3^n · 4^m.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Syntax:  p ::= atom | ⊥ | p → q,  with atoms ("btn", i) and ("sw", j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Atom = Tuple[str, int]
Formula = Tuple  # ("atom", Atom) | ("fls",) | ("imp", Formula, Formula)

FLS: Formula = ("fls",)


def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:
    """Atomic assertion: kind is 'btn' (a button) or 'sw' (a switch)."""
    return ("atom", (kind, index))


def imp(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Material implication p → q."""
    return ("imp", p, q)


def neg(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Negation ¬p := p → ⊥."""
    return imp(p, FLS)


TRU: Formula = neg(FLS)


def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Disjunction p ∨ q := ¬p → q."""
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def conj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Conjunction p ∧ q := ¬(p → ¬q)."""
    return neg(imp(p, neg(q)))


def show(p: Formula) -> str:
    """Human-readable rendering of a formula."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return "⊥"
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return ("b%d" % i) if kind == "btn" else ("s%d" % i)
    left, right = p[1], p[2]
    if right == FLS:
        return "¬" + show(left)
    return "(%s → %s)" % (show(left), show(right))


def atoms_of(p: Formula) -> List[Atom]:
    """All atoms occurring in p, without repetition, in order of appearance."""
    out: List[Atom] = []

    def walk(q: Formula) -> None:
        if q[0] == "atom":
            if q[1] not in out:
                out.append(q[1])
        elif q[0] == "imp":
            walk(q[1])
            walk(q[2])

    walk(p)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Layer A: Boolean values over the powerset algebra of generic objects
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def top_mask(m: int) -> int:
    """The element ⊤ of the algebra P({0,1}^m), as a bitmask of width 2^m."""
    return (1 << (1 << m)) - 1


def generic_objects(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All 2^m switch settings, indexed consistently with the bitmask order."""
    return [tuple(reversed(bits)) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def generic_index(g: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Index of the generic object g in the enumeration `generic_objects`."""
    return sum(bit << k for k, bit in enumerate(g))


def make_assignment(stage: FrozenSet[int], n: int, m: int) -> Dict[Atom, int]:
    """Stage-`stage` assignment of Boolean values to all atoms."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    assign: Dict[Atom, int] = {}
    for i in range(n):
        assign[("btn", i)] = full if i in stage else 0
    for j in range(m):
        mask = 0
        for idx, g in enumerate(generic_objects(m)):
            if g[j] == 1:
                mask |= 1 << idx
        assign[("sw", j)] = mask
    return assign


def bval(p: Formula, assign: Dict[Atom, int], m: int) -> int:
    """Boolean value ⟦p⟧ ∈ P({0,1}^m), computed by structural recursion."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return 0
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return assign[p[1]]
    a = bval(p[1], assign, m)
    b = bval(p[2], assign, m)
    return (full & ~a) | b  # a ⇒ b = aᶜ ∨ b


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Two-valued satisfaction at a control world
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], Tuple[int, ...]]


def csat(w: World, p: Formula) -> bool:
    """Two-valued truth of p at the control world w = (S, g)."""
    stage, g = w
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return False
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return (i in stage) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(w, p[1])) or csat(w, p[2])


def worlds(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All 2^(n+m) control worlds with n buttons and m switches."""
    out: List[World] = []
    for r in range(n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), r):
            for g in generic_objects(m):
                out.append((frozenset(combo), g))
    return out


def accessible(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Forcing accessibility: buttons may only be pushed, never unpushed."""
    return w[0] <= v[0]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Modal operators on predicates over a finite frame
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Pred = Callable[[World], bool]


def box(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def dia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def gbox(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground necessity: quantify over worlds of which w is an extension."""
    return lambda w: all(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def gdia(ws: Sequence[World], P: Pred) -> Pred:
    """Ground possibility."""
    return lambda w: any(P(v) for v in ws if accessible(v, w))


def all_predicates(ws: Sequence[World]) -> Iterable[Pred]:
    """All 2^|W| predicates on a finite frame (used for schematic validity)."""
    k = len(ws)
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(ws)}
    for mask in range(1 << k):
        yield (lambda mask=mask: (lambda w: bool(mask >> index[w] & 1)))()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 1 -- forcing closure: tautologies have Boolean value ⊤
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_forcing_closure(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. FORCING CLOSURE:  every classical tautology has Boolean value ⊤")
    print("=" * 74)
    p, q, r = atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)
    axioms = {
        "A1  p → (q → p)": imp(p, imp(q, p)),
        "A2  (p→(q→r)) → ((p→q)→(p→r))": imp(
            imp(p, imp(q, r)), imp(imp(p, q), imp(p, r))
        ),
        "A3  ¬¬p → p": imp(neg(neg(p)), p),
        "excluded middle  p ∨ ¬p": disj(p, neg(p)),
        "Peirce  ((p→q)→p)→p": imp(imp(imp(p, q), p), p),
    }
    full = top_mask(m)
    for stage in (frozenset(), frozenset({0}), frozenset({0, 1})):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
        for name, f in axioms.items():
            value = bval(f, assign, m)
            assert value == full, (name, stage, value)
    print("   all axioms and tautologies evaluate to ⊤ = %s at every stage" % bin(full))
    # a non-theorem does not:
    contingent = atom("sw", 0)
    assign = make_assignment(frozenset(), n, m)
    print("   by contrast ⟦s0⟧ = %s  (neither ⊥ nor ⊤)" % bin(bval(contingent, assign, m)))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 2 -- the truth lemma for principal generic filters
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_truth_lemma(n: int = 2, m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. TRUTH LEMMA:  quot(v,U_g) ⊨ p   iff   ⟦p⟧ ∈ U_g   (U_g principal at g)")
    print("=" * 74)
    formulas = _sample_formulas(n, m)
    checked = 0
    for stage in _stages(n):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
        for g in generic_objects(m):
            idx = generic_index(g)
            for f in formulas:
                value = bval(f, assign, m)
                in_filter = bool(value >> idx & 1)
                # the generic quotient by U_g has atomic diagram of (stage, g)
                assert csat((stage, g), f) == in_filter
                checked += 1
    print("   %d instances verified across %d stages and %d generic objects"
          % (checked, 2 ** n, 2 ** m))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 3 -- realization theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_realization(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. REALIZATION THEOREM:  (S,g) ⊨ p   iff   g ∈ ⟦p⟧_S")
    print("=" * 74)
    formulas = _sample_formulas(n, m)
    rows = 0
    for stage in _stages(n):
        assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
        for f in formulas:
            value = bval(f, assign, m)
            for g in generic_objects(m):
                assert csat((stage, g), f) == bool(value >> generic_index(g) & 1)
            rows += 1
    print("   %d (stage, formula) pairs verified; e.g." % rows)
    stage = frozenset({0})
    assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
    for f in [atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1), atom("sw", 0),
              conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0))]:
        print("      S={0}   ⟦%-14s⟧ = %s" % (show(f), bin(bval(f, assign, m))))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 4 -- frame laws, S4.2 soundness, and the failures of 5, B and .3
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_frame_logic(n: int = 2, m: int = 1) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. FRAME LAWS, S4.2 SOUNDNESS, AND THE FAILURE OF 5, B AND .3")
    print("=" * 74)
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    assert all(accessible(w, w) for w in ws)
    assert all(
        accessible(w, u)
        for w, v, u in product(ws, ws, ws)
        if accessible(w, v) and accessible(v, u)
    )
    directed = all(
        any(accessible(v1, u) and accessible(v2, u) for u in ws)
        for v1, v2 in product(ws, ws)
    )
    print("   reflexive: yes    transitive: yes    directed: %s" % directed)

    ok_T = ok_4 = ok_dot2 = True
    for P in all_predicates(ws):
        for w in ws:
            ok_T &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or P(w)
            ok_4 &= (not box(ws, P)(w)) or box(ws, box(ws, P))(w)
            ok_dot2 &= (not dia(ws, box(ws, P))(w)) or box(ws, dia(ws, P))(w)
    print("   T (□p→p): %s    4 (□p→□□p): %s    .2 (◇□p→□◇p): %s"
          % (ok_T, ok_4, ok_dot2))

    # axiom 5 and Brouwer fail for P = "button 0 is still unpushed"
    P_unpushed: Pred = lambda w: 0 not in w[0]
    w0: World = (frozenset(), generic_objects(m)[0])
    print("   counterexample predicate: 'button 0 unpushed', base world S=∅")
    print("      ◇P holds:            %s" % dia(ws, P_unpushed)(w0))
    print("      P holds:             %s" % P_unpushed(w0))
    print("      □◇P holds:           %s   ->  axiom 5 and Brouwer both FAIL"
          % box(ws, dia(ws, P_unpushed))(w0))

    # linearity .3 fails with two independent buttons
    P1: Pred = lambda w: 0 in w[0]
    P2: Pred = lambda w: 1 in w[0]
    left = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P1)(v)) or P2(v))(w0)
    right = box(ws, lambda v: (not box(ws, P2)(v)) or P1(v))(w0)
    print("      .3  □(□p→q) ∨ □(□q→p) at S=∅: %s ∨ %s = %s   ->  FAILS"
          % (left, right, left or right))

    # the mixed tense axiom p → □ ◇̌ p is valid on the same frame
    tense_ok = all(
        (not P(w)) or box(ws, gdia(ws, P))(w)
        for P in all_predicates(ws)
        for w in ws
    )
    print("   mixed tense axiom p → □◇̌p (ground modality): %s" % tense_ok)
    print("      => bimodal separation: □◇̌ valid while □◇ (Brouwer) fails")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 5 -- derived buttons and derived CH branches
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def demo_buttons_and_branches(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. DERIVED BUTTONS AND DERIVED CH BRANCHES")
    print("=" * 74)
    positive = [
        atom("btn", 0),
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)),
        conj(TRU, disj(atom("btn", 0), conj(atom("btn", 1), atom("btn", 0)))),
    ]
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    for f in positive:
        # Boolean-valued monotonicity along the stage order
        for S, T in product(_stages(n), _stages(n)):
            if S <= T:
                vs = bval(f, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
                vt = bval(f, make_assignment(T, n, m), m)
                assert vs & ~vt == 0, (show(f), S, T)
        # the resulting button law in the frame
        assert all(
            (not csat(w, f)) or csat(v, f)
            for w, v in product(ws, ws)
            if accessible(w, v)
        )
        print("   %-42s is a button (monotone Boolean value)" % show(f))

    ch = atom("sw", 0)  # the designated CH switch
    for S in _stages(n):
        value = bval(ch, make_assignment(S, n, m), m)
        assert value != 0 and value != top_mask(m)
    print("   ⟦CH⟧_S is neither ⊥ nor ⊤ at every stage -> branching theorem applies")
    for w in ws:
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: csat(v, ch))(w)
        assert dia(ws, lambda v: not csat(v, ch))(w)
    print("   ◇CH ∧ ◇¬CH holds at every one of the %d worlds: CH is a switch" % len(ws))
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 6 -- the invariant fragment theorem
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def button_free_normal_form(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    """Substitute ⊥ for every button atom: the canonical button-free candidate."""
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return p
    if p[0] == "atom":
        return FLS if p[1][0] == "btn" else p
    return imp(button_free_normal_form(p[1]), button_free_normal_form(p[2]))


def is_invariant(p: Formula, n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """Does the truth value of p depend only on the switch setting?"""
    for g in generic_objects(m):
        values = {csat((S, g), p) for S in _stages(n)}
        if len(values) > 1:
            return False
    return True


def demo_invariant_fragment(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. INVARIANT FRAGMENT THEOREM:  invariance ⟺ button-free normal form")
    print("=" * 74)
    tests = [
        atom("sw", 0),
        imp(atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1)),
        atom("btn", 0),
        disj(atom("btn", 0), neg(atom("btn", 0))),          # a tautology: invariant
        imp(atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 0)),                # invariant
        conj(atom("btn", 0), atom("sw", 0)),                # not invariant
    ]
    for p in tests:
        inv = is_invariant(p, n, m)
        nf = button_free_normal_form(p)
        agrees = all(
            csat((S, g), p) == csat((S, g), nf)
            for S in _stages(n)
            for g in generic_objects(m)
        )
        assert inv == agrees, show(p)
        print("   %-28s invariant=%-5s  normal form %-22s agrees=%s"
              % (show(p), inv, show(nf), agrees))
    print("   (equality of the two columns is exactly the fragment theorem)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 7 -- exact criterion for two-sided branch preservation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def survives_both_branches(background: int, value: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥ -- necessary and sufficient."""
    full = top_mask(m)
    return (background & value) != 0 and (background & full & ~value) != 0


def demo_branch_preservation(n: int = 2, m: int = 2) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. BRANCH PRESERVATION:  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ ≠ ⊥  and  b ∧ ⟦p⟧ᶜ ≠ ⊥")
    print("=" * 74)
    stage = frozenset({0})
    assign = make_assignment(stage, n, m)
    ch = atom("sw", 0)
    value = bval(ch, assign, m)
    cases = {
        "button background  ⟦b0⟧ (b0 pushed)": bval(atom("btn", 0), assign, m),
        "trivial background ⊤": top_mask(m),
        "switch background  ⟦s0⟧ = ⟦CH⟧": value,
        "opposite switch    ⟦¬s0⟧": bval(neg(ch), assign, m),
        "unpushed button    ⟦b1⟧": bval(atom("btn", 1), assign, m),
    }
    for name, b in cases.items():
        print("   %-38s  b=%-8s survives both CH branches: %s"
              % (name, bin(b), survives_both_branches(b, value, m)))
    print("   -> button-definable backgrounds branch; switch-entangled ones cannot,")
    print("      and an inconsistent background (⊥) branches vacuously nowhere.")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Demo 8 -- counting the frame:  3^n · 4^m accessibility pairs
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def count_accessibility_pairs(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of the pairs (w,v) with w ⊑ v."""
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    return sum(1 for w, v in product(ws, ws) if accessible(w, v))


def demo_counting(max_n: int = 3, max_m: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. EXACT SIZE OF THE FORCING RELATION:  |⊑| = 3^n · 4^m")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    n  m   worlds 2^(n+m)   brute force   3^n·4^m   match")
    for n in range(max_n + 1):
        for m in range(max_m + 1):
            if n + m > 5:
                continue
            brute = count_accessibility_pairs(n, m)
            closed = 3 ** n * 4 ** m
            assert brute == closed
            print("   %2d %2d   %12d   %11d   %7d   %s"
                  % (n, m, 2 ** (n + m), brute, closed, brute == closed))
    print("   three states per button (off/off, off/on, on/on -- never on/off),")
    print("   four per switch (its value before and after are unconstrained).")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  helpers
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def _stages(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """All 2^n stages (sets of pushed buttons)."""
    return [
        frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)
    ]


def _sample_formulas(n: int, m: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """A spread of test formulas mixing button and switch atoms."""
    b0, b1 = atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", min(1, n - 1))
    s0, s1 = atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", min(1, m - 1))
    return [
        FLS,
        TRU,
        b0,
        s0,
        neg(b0),
        neg(s0),
        imp(b0, s0),
        conj(b0, s0),
        disj(b0, s0),
        conj(disj(b0, b1), neg(s1)),
        imp(conj(s0, s1), disj(b0, neg(b1))),
    ]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("BOOLEAN-VALUED REALIZATION OF THE FORCING MULTIVERSE -- NUMERICAL DEMOS")
    print()
    demo_forcing_closure()
    demo_truth_lemma()
    demo_realization()
    demo_frame_logic()
    demo_buttons_and_branches()
    demo_invariant_fragment()
    demo_branch_preservation()
    demo_counting()
    print("all checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Bitmask Evaluation of Boolean Values and the Realization Test
algorithms.description: Computes the Boolean value of a propositional assertion in the powerset algebra of the space of generic objects, and verifies the realization theorem pointwise. The algebra is the powerset of G = {0,1}^m, represented as integer bitmasks of width 2^m, so meet, join, complement and Heyting implication are single bitwise operations. At stage S a pushed button atom receives the top mask, an unpushed one the zero mask, and switch j receives the mask of generic objects turning it on; the value of a compound assertion is then computed by structural recursion using a implies b = complement(a) or b. Evaluating an assertion of size |p| costs O(|p|) bitwise operations on 2^m-bit integers, i.e. O(|p| * 2^m / w) machine operations for word size w. The realization test compares, for each of the 2^m generic objects, ordinary two-valued satisfaction at the control world (S,g) with the g-th bit of the Boolean value; agreement across all g is precisely the statement of the realization theorem at stage S. This routine is the computational core on which the branching, button and invariance tests are built.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: assertion p; stage S subset of {0..n-1}; parameters n, m
OUTPUT: Boolean value [[p]]_S as a bitmask of width 2^m

1. FULL <- 2^(2^m) - 1                       // the top element of the algebra
2. for each generic object g in {0,1}^m:
3.     idx(g) <- sum over k of g[k] * 2^k    // bit position assigned to g
4. for i in 0..n-1:                          // stage assignment, buttons
5.     assign[btn i] <- FULL if i in S else 0
6. for j in 0..m-1:                          // stage assignment, switches
7.     assign[sw j] <- OR over g with g[j]=1 of (1 << idx(g))
8. function VALUE(q):
9.     if q = bottom            return 0
10.    if q = atom a            return assign[a]
11.    if q = (r -> s)          return (FULL AND NOT VALUE(r)) OR VALUE(s)
12. V <- VALUE(p)
13. // realization check
14. for each generic object g:
15.     assert TWOVALUED(S, g, p) = ((V >> idx(g)) AND 1)
16. return V

algorithms.name: Enumeration of the Control Frame and the 3^n * 4^m Accessibility Count
algorithms.description: Enumerates every world of the n-button, m-switch forcing frame and counts the pairs of the accessibility relation, confirming the closed form 3^n * 4^m against brute force. A world is a pair (S,g) with S a set of pushed buttons and g a switch setting, and (S,g) is accessible to (T,h) exactly when S is a subset of T -- buttons may be pushed but never unpushed, while switches are unconstrained. Brute-force counting enumerates the 2^(n+m) worlds and performs a subset test on each of the 4^(n+m) ordered pairs. The closed form is derived from the enumerative identity sum over T subset of [n] of 2^|T| = 3^n: each button occupies one of three states across an accessible pair (off/off, off/on, on/on -- the state on/off being forbidden by irreversibility), while each switch occupies one of four. The routine also verifies the underlying subset-sum identity directly, and the two computations together exhibit the exponents 3 and 4 as the arithmetical signature of irreversibility versus freedom.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: n buttons, m switches
OUTPUT: number of accessibility pairs, by brute force and in closed form

1. STAGES  <- all 2^n subsets of {0..n-1}
2. SETTINGS<- all 2^m functions {0..m-1} -> {0,1}
3. W       <- { (S,g) : S in STAGES, g in SETTINGS }      // 2^(n+m) worlds
4. count <- 0
5. for each w = (S,g) in W:
6.     for each v = (T,h) in W:
7.         if S subset of T then count <- count + 1
8. closed <- 3^n * 4^m
9. assert count = closed
10. // the identity behind the closed form
11. assert sum over T in STAGES of 2^|T| = 3^n
12. return (count, closed)
algorithms.code:
"""
Enumeration of the finite button-switch control frame and verification of the
closed form |⊑| = 3^n · 4^m for the number of accessibility pairs.

Worlds are pairs (S, g) with S ⊆ {0,...,n-1} the set of pushed buttons and
g ∈ {0,1}^m a switch setting; (S,g) ⊑ (T,h) iff S ⊆ T.  Brute-force counting is
O(4^(n+m)) subset tests; the closed form is O(1).  The proof behind the closed
form is the identity  Σ_{T ⊆ [n]} 2^|T| = 3^n:  each button occupies one of
three states in an accessible pair (off/off, off/on, on/on -- never on/off),
each switch one of four.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import FrozenSet, List, Tuple

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], Tuple[int, ...]]


def stages(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """All 2^n sets of pushed buttons."""
    return [frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)]


def settings(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All 2^m switch settings."""
    return [tuple(reversed(bits)) for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def worlds(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All 2^(n+m) control worlds."""
    return [(S, g) for S in stages(n) for g in settings(m)]


def accessible(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Forcing accessibility: buttons may only be pushed, never unpushed."""
    return w[0] <= v[0]


def count_pairs_bruteforce(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Count the pairs (w,v) with w ⊑ v by exhaustive enumeration."""
    ws = worlds(n, m)
    return sum(1 for w in ws for v in ws if accessible(w, v))


def count_pairs_closed_form(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """The closed form 3^n · 4^m."""
    return 3 ** n * 4 ** m


def subset_sum_identity(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The enumerative heart: Σ_{T ⊆ [n]} 2^|T| = 3^n."""
    lhs = sum(2 ** len(T) for T in stages(n))
    return lhs, 3 ** n


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(" n  m   worlds   brute force   3^n*4^m")
    for n in range(4):
        for m in range(4):
            if n + m > 5:
                continue
            brute = count_pairs_bruteforce(n, m)
            closed = count_pairs_closed_form(n, m)
            assert brute == closed
            print("%2d %2d %8d %13d %9d" % (n, m, 2 ** (n + m), brute, closed))
    for n in range(6):
        lhs, rhs = subset_sum_identity(n)
        assert lhs == rhs
    print("subset-sum identity verified for n <= 5")

algorithms.name: Schematic Modal Validity Checking on Finite Forcing Frames
algorithms.description: Decides whether a modal schema is valid on a finite control frame by quantifying over every predicate that may be substituted for its schematic letters. Validity of a modal schema is not a statement about one valuation but about all of them, so on a frame with |W| worlds the checker iterates over the 2^|W| predicates per schematic letter, evaluating the box and diamond operators by scanning successors: a one-letter schema costs O(2^|W| * |W|^2) and a two-letter schema such as linearity costs O(4^|W| * |W|^2). This is exponential in the size of the frame but immediate for the small frames that carry the canonical countermodels. The checker confirms that T, 4 and .2 are valid on every control frame -- so the frame is sound for S4.2 -- that the axioms 5 and Brouwer fail as soon as a single button is present, that linearity .3 fails as soon as two independent buttons are present, and that the mixed tense law p -> box gdia p, whose diamond looks downward to grounds, is valid on exactly the frames where its unimodal analogue fails. Combined with soundness of a Hilbert calculus for S4.2 on all directed preorders, each refutation is an independence proof.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: frame parameters n, m; schema name X in {T, 4, .2, 5, B, tense, .3}
OUTPUT: (valid?, refuting witness if any)

1. W <- all worlds (S,g);  ACC(w,v) <- (w.S subset of v.S)
2. BOX(P)(w)  <- for all v in W with ACC(w,v): P(v)
3. DIA(P)(w)  <- exists v in W with ACC(w,v) and P(v)
4. GDIA(P)(w) <- exists v in W with ACC(v,w) and P(v)      // ground possibility
5. if X has one schematic letter:
6.     for each of the 2^|W| predicates P:
7.         for each w in W:
8.             evaluate the instance of X at w
9.             if it is false: return (false, witness (w,P))
10.    return (true, none)
11. if X = .3:
12.    for each pair of predicates (P,Q) and each w in W:
13.        L <- BOX(v -> (not BOX(P)(v)) or Q(v))(w)
14.        R <- BOX(v -> (not BOX(Q)(v)) or P(v))(w)
15.        if not (L or R): return (false, witness (w,P,Q))
16.    return (true, none)

algorithms.name: Deciding Multiverse Invariance and Two-Sided Branch Preservation
algorithms.description: Two decision procedures drawn from the sharp characterizations of the theory. The first decides whether an assertion is multiverse-invariant -- preserved both by passing to forcing extensions and by passing back down to grounds. By the invariant fragment theorem this holds exactly when the assertion is equivalent to a button-free one, and the theorem supplies a canonical witness: substitute falsity for every button atom. Normalization is O(|p|) and confirming agreement across the frame is O(|p| * 2^(n+m)), which is strictly cheaper than searching for an equivalent button-free assertion; the routine returns the witness when the verdict is positive. The second decides whether a background condition survives into both a p-branch and a not-p-branch of one and the same Boolean-valued universe. The exact criterion -- necessary as well as sufficient -- is that the background meet both the Boolean value of p and its complement, which is two bitwise-and tests, hence O(1) word operations. Applied to the control frame it separates button-definable backgrounds, which always branch, from switch-entangled ones, which provably cannot.
algorithms.pseudocode:
PART A -- invariance
INPUT: assertion p; frame parameters n, m
OUTPUT: (invariant?, button-free witness)
1. function NF(q):                        // substitute bottom for button atoms
2.     if q = bottom            return bottom
3.     if q = atom (btn i)      return bottom
4.     if q = atom (sw j)       return q
5.     if q = (r -> s)          return (NF(r) -> NF(s))
6. nf <- NF(p)
7. agrees <- for all stages S and settings g: TRUTH(S,g,p) = TRUTH(S,g,nf)
8. return (agrees, nf if agrees else none)

PART B -- two-sided branch preservation
INPUT: background bitmask b; Boolean value V of the varied assertion; m
OUTPUT: whether b survives into both branches
9.  FULL <- 2^(2^m) - 1
10. return (b AND V) /= 0  and  (b AND FULL AND NOT V) /= 0

visualizations.name: The Forcing Multiverse as a Control Panel: Hasse Diagram of the Two-Button, One-Switch Frame
visualizations.description: A layered drawing of the eight worlds of the two-button, one-switch forcing frame. Vertical position is the number of buttons pushed, so the order climbs and never descends; grey arrows are the covering steps of accessibility (pushing one further button) and red double arrows are the free switch moves inside a stage. Colour encodes the value of the designated switch, the Continuum Hypothesis. The picture displays three theorems at once: irreversibility of buttons, directedness (every two worlds have a common world above them, which is the semantic content of the axiom .2), and the switch property of the Continuum Hypothesis, since both colours occur above every world. The bottom stage, with no button pushed, is the analogue of the mantle: a ground of every world.
visualizations.code:
"""
The forcing multiverse as a control panel: Hasse diagram of the 2-button,
1-switch frame.

Worlds are pairs (S, g).  Vertical position is the number of pushed buttons
(irreversible progress); horizontal position separates the switch settings.
Solid arrows are the covering steps of the accessibility relation: pushing one
further button, or flipping the switch (a move within a stage, drawn as a
horizontal double arrow).  Colour encodes the value of the designated switch
(the Continuum Hypothesis): blue = CH true, orange = CH false.

The picture makes three theorems visible at once: the order climbs and never
descends (buttons are irreversible), every pair of worlds has an upper bound
(directedness, hence the axiom .2), and both colours occur above every world
(CH is a switch, so both branches remain permanently available).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, List, Tuple

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

World = Tuple[FrozenSet[int], int]

N_BUTTONS = 2


def stages(n: int) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    return [frozenset(c) for r in range(n + 1) for c in combinations(range(n), r)]


def layout(n: int) -> Dict[World, Tuple[float, float]]:
    pos: Dict[World, Tuple[float, float]] = {}
    by_level: Dict[int, List[FrozenSet[int]]] = {}
    for S in stages(n):
        by_level.setdefault(len(S), []).append(S)
    for level, group in by_level.items():
        for k, S in enumerate(sorted(group, key=lambda s: sorted(s))):
            centre = (k - (len(group) - 1) / 2) * 3.4
            for ch in (0, 1):
                pos[(S, ch)] = (centre + (0.72 if ch else -0.72), float(level))
    return pos


def label(S: FrozenSet[int], ch: int) -> str:
    pushed = "".join("b%d" % i for i in sorted(S)) or "-"
    return "%s\n%s" % (pushed, "CH" if ch else "¬CH")


def main() -> None:
    pos = layout(N_BUTTONS)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 7))

    # covering steps: push exactly one further button (switch may change freely)
    for (S, ch), (x, y) in pos.items():
        for (T, ch2), (x2, y2) in pos.items():
            if len(T) == len(S) + 1 and S < T:
                ax.annotate("", xy=(x2, y2 - 0.08), xytext=(x, y + 0.08),
                            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#8899aa",
                                            lw=1.0, alpha=0.75))
        # the switch move inside a stage
        if ch == 0:
            x2, y2 = pos[(S, 1)]
            ax.annotate("", xy=(x2 - 0.28, y2), xytext=(x + 0.28, y),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<|-|>", color="#c0392b", lw=1.6))

    for (S, ch), (x, y) in pos.items():
        colour = "#2d6cdf" if ch else "#e08a1e"
        ax.scatter([x], [y], s=1500, c=colour, edgecolors="black",
                   zorder=3, alpha=0.92)
        ax.text(x, y, label(S, ch), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                color="white", zorder=4, fontweight="bold")

    ax.text(-4.6, 0.0, "mantle:\nno button pushed", fontsize=9, style="italic",
            ha="left", va="center")
    ax.set_title("The forcing multiverse of 2 buttons and 1 switch\n"
                 "grey arrows: push a button (irreversible)   "
                 "red arrows: flip the switch (free, forever)",
                 fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel("number of buttons pushed")
    ax.set_yticks([0, 1, 2])
    ax.set_xticks([])
    for side in ("top", "right", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xlim(-5.0, 5.0)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 2.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("multiverse_frame.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote multiverse_frame.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Irreversibility versus Freedom: Growth and Density of the Accessibility Relation
visualizations.description: Two panels quantifying the difference between a button and a switch. The left panel plots, on a logarithmic scale, the exact number of accessibility pairs of the n-button, m-switch frame -- 3^n for pure buttons, 4^m for pure switches -- against the number of worlds 2^k. The right panel plots the density of the relation, the number of accessible pairs divided by the number of all pairs, which equals (3/4)^n and is completely independent of the number of switches. The two curves make the combinatorial content of the counting theorem visible: each button removes exactly one of the four possible states of a pair (the state pushed-then-unpushed, forbidden by the no-undo rule) while each switch keeps all four.
visualizations.code:
"""
Counting the multiverse: irreversibility versus freedom.

Left panel: the exact number of accessibility pairs of the n-button, m-switch
control frame, 3^n · 4^m, compared with the number of worlds 2^(n+m) and with
the number of all pairs 4^(n+m).  Buttons contribute a factor 3 per unit
(off/off, off/on, on/on -- the fourth combination on/off is forbidden by
irreversibility) whereas switches contribute the full factor 4.

Right panel: the density |⊑| / |W|^2 = (3/4)^n, showing that switches never
thin out the relation while each button removes a fixed quarter of the possible
pairs.  The exponent 3 is the arithmetical signature of the no-undo rule.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def pairs(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of accessible pairs."""
    return 3 ** n * 4 ** m


def main() -> None:
    ks: List[int] = list(range(0, 9))
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))

    ax1.semilogy(ks, [pairs(k, 0) for k in ks], "o-", color="#2d6cdf",
                 label=r"$k$ buttons: $3^k$ pairs")
    ax1.semilogy(ks, [pairs(0, k) for k in ks], "s-", color="#e08a1e",
                 label=r"$k$ switches: $4^k$ pairs")
    ax1.semilogy(ks, [2 ** k for k in ks], "^--", color="#666666",
                 label=r"worlds: $2^k$")
    ax1.set_xlabel("number of controls $k$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("count (log scale)")
    ax1.set_title("Size of the accessibility relation")
    ax1.legend()
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

    for m in range(4):
        density = [pairs(n, m) / (2 ** (n + m)) ** 2 for n in ks]
        ax2.plot(ks, density, "o-", label="%d switch%s" % (m, "" if m == 1 else "es"))
    ax2.set_xlabel("number of buttons $n$")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$|\sqsubseteq| \, / \, |W|^2$")
    ax2.set_title(r"Density of the relation is $(3/4)^n$, independent of $m$")
    ax2.legend()
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    fig.suptitle("Irreversibility costs a factor 3 per button; freedom keeps 4 per switch")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("multiverse_counting.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote multiverse_counting.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Boolean Values as Sets of Generic Objects: the Realization Theorem as a Heat Map
visualizations.description: A heat map of Boolean values at a fixed stage. Each row is an assertion, each column a generic object (a switch setting), and a filled cell means the generic object belongs to the Boolean value of the assertion -- equivalently, by the realization theorem, that the corresponding control world satisfies the assertion. Button assertions produce rows that are uniformly filled or uniformly empty, since a button is decided outright at each stage; switch assertions produce genuinely mixed rows. A mixed row is precisely a Boolean value that is neither bottom nor top, so by the branching theorem it is true in one generic quotient and false in another: the mixed rows of this picture are the branches of the multiverse.
visualizations.code:
"""
Boolean values and the realization theorem, drawn as a heat map.

For a fixed stage S (a set of pushed buttons) each assertion p has a Boolean
value ⟦p⟧_S, a *set of generic objects*.  The realization theorem says that the
two-valued world (S,g) satisfies p exactly when the generic object g lies in
that set.  Each row of the picture is one assertion; each column is one generic
object (a switch setting); a filled cell means the generic object belongs to the
Boolean value, i.e. the corresponding world satisfies the assertion.

Button assertions produce rows that are entirely filled or entirely empty --
a button is decided outright at each stage.  Switch assertions produce genuinely
mixed rows, and a mixed row is precisely a value that is neither ⊥ nor ⊤: by the
Branching Theorem such an assertion is true in one generic quotient and false in
another.  Those mixed rows are the branches of the multiverse.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Atom = Tuple[str, int]
Formula = Tuple
FLS: Formula = ("fls",)

M_SWITCHES = 3
N_BUTTONS = 2


def atom(kind: str, index: int) -> Formula:
    return ("atom", (kind, index))


def imp(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("imp", p, q)


def neg(p: Formula) -> Formula:
    return imp(p, FLS)


def conj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return neg(imp(p, neg(q)))


def disj(p: Formula, q: Formula) -> Formula:
    return imp(neg(p), q)


def generics(m: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    return [tuple(reversed(b)) for b in product((0, 1), repeat=m)]


def csat(S: FrozenSet[int], g: Sequence[int], p: Formula) -> bool:
    if p[0] == "fls":
        return False
    if p[0] == "atom":
        kind, i = p[1]
        return (i in S) if kind == "btn" else (g[i] == 1)
    return (not csat(S, g, p[1])) or csat(S, g, p[2])


def main() -> None:
    b0, b1 = atom("btn", 0), atom("btn", 1)
    s0, s1, s2 = atom("sw", 0), atom("sw", 1), atom("sw", 2)
    rows: List[Tuple[str, Formula]] = [
        ("⊥", FLS),
        ("⊤", neg(FLS)),
        ("b0  (button)", b0),
        ("b1  (button)", b1),
        ("b0 ∧ b1", conj(b0, b1)),
        ("CH = s0  (switch)", s0),
        ("¬CH", neg(s0)),
        ("CH ∧ s1", conj(s0, s1)),
        ("CH ∨ s2", disj(s0, s2)),
        ("b0 → CH", imp(b0, s0)),
        ("b0 ∧ CH", conj(b0, s0)),
    ]
    stage = frozenset({0})
    gs = generics(M_SWITCHES)
    data = np.array([[1.0 if csat(stage, g, p) else 0.0 for g in gs]
                     for _, p in rows])

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.6))
    ax.imshow(data, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1.35, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(gs)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(["".join(str(b) for b in g) for g in gs], fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([name for name, _ in rows], fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("generic object $g$ (switch setting $s_0 s_1 s_2$)")
    ax.set_title("Boolean values at stage $S=\\{b_0\\}$:  filled cell  ⟺  "

    for i in range(len(rows)):

            ax.text(j, i, "1" if data[i, j] else "0", ha="center", va="center",

interactive_demos.description: A live model of the forcing multiverse with two irreversible buttons and two free switches, one of them designated as the Continuum Hypothesis. Pushing a button is permanent -- the only way back is to rebuild the universe from the mantle -- while flipping a switch costs nothing and is always available again. The panel renders the sixteen-world frame as a layered graph with the current universe highlighted and the universes it can still reach picked out, and it reports how many of them remain. An assertion analyser accepts any propositional formula in the button and switch atoms and reports live: its truth here, whether it necessarily holds in every forcing extension, whether it is possible, whether it holds in some ground, whether it is a button, whether it is a switch, whether it is multiverse-invariant, and whether the axiom 5, the Brouwer axiom and the mixed tense law hold for it at the current universe. A Boolean value table shows the assertion's value at the current stage as an explicit set of generic objects, flagging uniform values as decided and mixed values as branching. Three experiments make the theory click: watch the axiom 5 die by typing the assertion 'button b0 is unpushed' and then pushing b0; confirm that the Continuum Hypothesis is flagged a switch at every world; and compare the invariance flag for an assertion mentioning a button against one that does not.
interactive_demos.html:
The Multiverse Control Panel

Two buttons and two switches. A button, once pushed, can never be unpushed — it models a set-theoretic assertion that forcing can achieve but never undo. A switch can be flipped up and down forever — it models the Continuum Hypothesis. A world is a pair (set of pushed buttons, switch setting), and a world can reach another exactly when the second has pushed at least the same buttons. Push, flip, and watch the logic of forcing appear.

Current universe

buttons  switches 
Pushing a button is permanent: the only way back is to rebuild the universe from the mantle. Flipping a switch costs nothing and is always available again.

The frame

Rows are stages (how many buttons are pushed); each node is one world. The highlighted node is your current universe, light nodes are the universes it can reach. Every two nodes have a common node above them — that is directedness, the semantic content of the axiom .2.

Assertion analyser

Syntax: atoms b0 b1 s0 s1, connectives ~ & | ->, parentheses. Try b0, s0, ~b0, b0 | b1, s0 -> s1, b0 & s0.

Boolean value at this stage  ⟦p⟧S

The Boolean value of an assertion at stage S is a set of generic objects — a set of switch settings. The Realization Theorem says the world (S, g) satisfies p exactly when g belongs to that set, so the table below is the truth of p across the switch fibre. A row of all 1s is ⊤, all 0s is ⊥; anything mixed is an assertion the universe has not decided, and by the Branching Theorem it is true in one generic quotient and false in another.

Modal diagnostics for your assertion

□p: true in every reachable universe. ◇p: true in some reachable universe. Button: p → □p holds everywhere. Switch: ◇p and ◇¬p hold everywhere. Invariant: the truth value never changes when only buttons change — by the Invariant Fragment Theorem, exactly the assertions equivalent to button-free ones. Axiom 5 (◇p → □◇p) and Brouwer (p → □◇p) fail precisely because a pushed button kills a possibility forever. Ground possibility ◇̌p looks downward, to universes of which this one is a forcing extension; the mixed law p → □◇̌p never fails, even though p → □◇p does.

# Buttons, Switches, and the Shape of the Mathematical Multiverse *A guided tour of the Boolean-valued realization of the forcing multiverse.* --- ## 1. The question behind the machine At the foundations of mathematics sits set theory, and the most famous question it cannot answer is the [Continuum Hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuum_hypothesis): is there a size of infinity strictly between the whole numbers and the real line? The standard axioms can neither prove nor refute it, and the technique that established this — [forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forcing_(mathematics)) — does something remarkable. It manufactures, from one universe of sets, a *larger* one in which a chosen statement becomes true. Forcing can be iterated. From any universe you may force, and force again. What emerges is not a single mathematical reality but a network of them: the **set-theoretic multiverse**. And once you have a network, a new question appears — not "is this true?" but "is this true *no matter where you go*?" Write $\Box p$ for "$p$ holds in every forcing extension" and $\Diamond p$ for "$p$ holds in some forcing extension". The **modal logic of forcing** asks which combinations of these operators are universally valid.
Why modal logic, of all things? (click to expand) Because forcing behaves exactly like an accessibility relation between possible worlds. The trivial forcing changes nothing, so every universe is accessible from itself (reflexivity). An iteration of forcings is again a forcing, so accessibility is transitive. And any two forcing extensions of a universe can be amalgamated into a common further extension, by forcing with the product of the two notions of forcing — a property called *directedness*. These three conditions are precisely the frame conditions of the modal system [$\mathsf{S4.2}$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_modal_logic).
--- ## 2. The control panel Here is the picture the entire theory turns out to be about. Some assertions, once forced true, can never be made false again — forcing only ever *adds* objects. Call these **buttons**: once pushed, pushed forever. Others can be forced true and then forced false, endlessly. Call these **switches**; the Continuum Hypothesis is the canonical one. A **world** is then a pair $(S, g)$: the finite set $S$ of buttons pushed so far, together with a setting $g$ of all the switches. World $(S,g)$ can reach $(T,h)$ exactly when $S \subseteq T$. Play with it. Push a button and watch a possibility disappear forever; flip a switch and watch nothing be lost at all. {{interactive_demo:0}} Three things are worth doing in the panel before reading on: 1. Type `~b0` (button $b_0$ is *not* pushed) at the mantle, note that $\Diamond p$ holds — then push $b_0$ and watch $\Box\Diamond p$ collapse. **That is the death of the axiom $5$.** 2. Type `s0` and confirm it is flagged a *switch* — both $\Diamond \mathrm{CH}$ and $\Diamond \neg\mathrm{CH}$ hold at every single world. 3. Type `b0 & s0` and then `s0 -> s1`, and compare the *invariant* flag. Only the second is invariant, because only it never mentions a button. --- ## 3. The frame, drawn Rows are stages: how many buttons have been pushed. The order climbs and never descends. Every pair of worlds has a common world above it — that is directedness — and both colours occur above every world, which is exactly the statement that the Continuum Hypothesis is a switch. {{visualization:0}}
The formal frame laws **Reflexivity.** $S \subseteq S$. **Transitivity.** $S \subseteq T \subseteq U$ gives $S \subseteq U$. **Directedness.** Given $(S_1,g_1)$ and $(S_2,g_2)$, the world $(S_1 \cup S_2, g_1)$ is above both. Note this is *unconditional*: any two worlds have an upper bound. These three yield the axioms $T$ ($\Box p \to p$), $4$ ($\Box p \to \Box\Box p$) and $.2$ ($\Diamond\Box p \to \Box\Diamond p$) respectively — the system $\mathsf{S4.2}$.
--- ## 4. From picture to construction: Boolean values So far this is a nice picture. A picture is not a theorem. The real question is whether one can *build* a mathematical structure in which all of these laws hold as consequences rather than stipulations. The tool is [Boolean-valued models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean-valued_model), the algebraic face of forcing. Instead of asking whether a statement is true or false, assign it a value $\llbracket p \rrbracket$ in a Boolean algebra of "degrees of truth": $$\llbracket \bot \rrbracket = \bot, \qquad \llbracket p \to q \rrbracket = \llbracket p \rrbracket \Rightarrow \llbracket q \rrbracket, \qquad a \Rightarrow b := a^{\complement} \vee b.$$ Two theorems make this a genuine semantics for forcing. > **Forcing Closure.** Every theorem of classical propositional logic receives value $\top$, in > every Boolean-valued universe. > **Truth Lemma.** Choose a **generic filter** $U$ — a set of Boolean values containing $\top$, > omitting $\bot$, closed upward and under meets, and *deciding* every element in the sense that > $a \in U$ or $a^{\complement} \in U$. Collapse the universe by declaring an atom true exactly > when its value lies in $U$. Then for *every* assertion, $p$ is true in this **generic quotient** > iff $\llbracket p \rrbracket \in U$.
Proof sketches *Forcing closure* is an induction on Hilbert-style derivations. It suffices that the three axiom schemes become Boolean identities — each provable by the residuation law $c \le a \Rightarrow b \iff c \wedge a \le b$ — and that modus ponens is sound, which follows from $a \wedge (a \Rightarrow b) \le b$. *The truth lemma* is an induction on formulas. The only content is that a generic filter respects Boolean implication: $a \Rightarrow b \in U$ iff ($a \in U$ implies $b \in U$). Left to right uses $a \wedge (a\Rightarrow b) \le b$; right to left splits on whether $a \in U$, using decisiveness in the negative case.
The algorithm below is the truth lemma made executable: Boolean values as bitmasks over the space of generic objects. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 5. Independence, for free Here is the payoff of the algebraic view. Suppose an assertion has a value that is *neither* $\bot$ nor $\top$, and suppose the algebra is **rich**: every nonzero element belongs to some generic filter. (For a powerset algebra this is free — take the principal filter at any point.) > **Branching Theorem.** If $\llbracket p \rrbracket \notin \{\bot, \top\}$, there are two generic > filters whose quotients disagree about $p$: one satisfies it, the other refutes it. Independence is no longer two separate constructions. It is the shadow of a single element of a Boolean algebra failing to be $0$ or $1$. The heat map below makes this visible. Each row is an assertion; each column a generic object; a filled cell means the corresponding world satisfies the assertion. Uniform rows are decided; mixed rows *are* the branches of the multiverse. {{visualization:2}} --- ## 6. The realization: the panel *is* a Boolean-valued universe Now close the loop. Take the Boolean algebra to be the powerset of the space $\mathcal{G}$ of switch settings. At stage $S$, a pushed button gets value $\mathcal{G}$, an unpushed one $\varnothing$, and switch $s$ gets $\{ g : g(s) = 1\}$. > **Realization Theorem.** For every stage $S$, every generic object $g$ and every assertion $p$, > $$(S,g) \models p \iff g \in \llbracket p \rrbracket_S .$$ The hand-drawn world $(S,g)$ *is* the generic quotient of the stage-$S$ Boolean-valued universe by the principal generic filter at $g$. And now the frame laws stop being assumptions: - **Buttons are derived.** Assertions built from button atoms by $\wedge$ and $\vee$ have Boolean values monotone in the stage, so by the realization theorem they satisfy $p \to \Box p$. - **Both CH branches are derived.** The value of the CH switch is neither empty (the all-on generic object is in it) nor everything (the all-off one is not), so the Branching Theorem applies verbatim. - **Directedness is derived** from the union of stages, which on the algebra side is the join of Boolean values.
Why this matters: the falsifiable obligation An abstract theory may simply *postulate* that the multiverse frame is directed and carries buttons and switches. The realization theorem discharges the corresponding obligation: there is *one* satisfaction relation, arising from an honest construction, for which reflexivity, transitivity, directedness, the button law, the switch law and both branch conditions all hold simultaneously. Had any one of them failed, the construction would have refuted the abstract frame.
--- ## 7. Exactly $\mathsf{S4.2}$ — no more, no less The logic is pinned down from both sides. - **$.2$ is exactly directedness.** If the schema $\Diamond \Box p \to \Box \Diamond p$ holds for *every* predicate, then the frame must be directed. (Apply it to the predicate "$y$ can reach me".) - **The frame validates $5$ if and only if there are no buttons.** One button suffices to kill $\mathsf{S5}$: let $p$ say "$b$ is unpushed"; at the mantle $\Diamond p$ holds, but after pushing $b$ it never can again. - **Two independent buttons refute linearity $.3$.** Push $b_1$ alone and $b_2$ alone: neither disjunct of $\Box(\Box p \to q) \vee \Box(\Box q \to p)$ survives. The multiverse genuinely branches; it is not a chain. Because a Hilbert calculus for $\mathsf{S4.2}$ can be proved sound on *every* directed preorder, each of these finite refutations doubles as an **independence proof**: neither $5$ nor $.3$ is a theorem of $\mathsf{S4.2}$. The checker below verifies all of this by brute force over every predicate on a finite frame. {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 8. What is true *everywhere*? A multiverse invites a notion of truth stronger than "true here". Which assertions never change value as you move around? > **Invariant Fragment Theorem.** An assertion has the same truth value at all worlds sharing a > switch setting — i.e. it is preserved by forcing extensions *and* by passing back down to > grounds — **iff** it is equivalent to a **button-free** assertion, one built from switch atoms > alone.
The proof, in one move Given an invariant $p$, substitute $\bot$ for every button atom. The result $p^{\bot}$ is button-free by construction, and an induction shows it computes the truth value of $p$ at the empty stage. Invariance transfers that value to every stage, so $p$ and $p^{\bot}$ agree everywhere. Sharpness is immediate: a bare button atom changes value when the button is pushed, so it is not invariant.
The lesson generalizes: preservation *upward* alone gives necessity above a world, not truth throughout the multiverse. Genuine invariance is **bidirectional**. That motivates a second modality $\check{\Diamond}$, reading "in some *ground*" — some universe of which this one is a forcing extension. On the very same frame: $$p \to \Box\,\check{\Diamond}\,p \quad \text{is valid}, \qquad\text{while}\qquad p \to \Box \Diamond p \quad\text{fails}.$$ So the two-way logic of the multiverse is strictly richer than the one-way logic of forcing. (You can test both lines live in the control panel above.) {{algorithm:3}} --- ## 9. Counting the panel A last, concrete fact with a pretty proof. > With $n$ buttons and $m$ switches, the frame has $2^{n+m}$ worlds and exactly $3^n \cdot 4^m$ > accessible pairs. Each button contributes three states to an accessible pair $(w,v)$: unpushed in both, pushed in $v$ only, pushed in both. The fourth combination — pushed in $w$ but not in $v$ — is exactly what the no-undo rule forbids. Each switch contributes four, since its value before and after is unconstrained. The identity behind it is $\sum_{t \subseteq s} 2^{|t|} = 3^{|s|}$. {{visualization:1}} {{algorithm:1}} --- ## 10. Run everything The full suite below verifies, by exhaustive finite computation, every theorem in this tour: forcing closure, the truth lemma, the realization theorem, the frame laws and the failures of $5$, $\mathrm{B}$ and $.3$, derived buttons, derived CH branches, the invariant fragment theorem, the branch-preservation criterion, and the count $3^n 4^m$. {{demo:0}} --- ## Where this leaves us None of this decides the Continuum Hypothesis; it was never going to. What it does is change the register of the question. Instead of asking which statements are true, we get a precise account of how truth *moves*: which assertions lock in, which oscillate forever, which are invisible to the motion, and exactly which laws of necessity and possibility that motion obeys. And the account is not a picture with a story attached. The control panel of irreversible buttons and free switches is a generic quotient of a Boolean-valued universe — a forcing construction, in disguise.
